newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Amoy 1995/96 net disappointing - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Amoy 1995/96 net disappointing - analysts.

text.p: Slow rental income growth at property investment company Amoy Properties Ltd led to disappointing earnings growth at the company in 1995/96, analysts said.
Amoy Properties posted net profit of HK$1.58 billion for the year ended June 30 compared to HK$1.55 billion the previous year. Earnings per share fell to 63.3 cents compared to 66.6 cents.
"The results were not really exciting," said Adrian Ngan, director at Peregrine Securities.
"There was a slow down in rental income and last year they did not have any property sales," he said
Ngan said he would be revising down his 1996/97 earnings estimates for the company to about HK$1.70-1.75 billion from a previous estimate of HK$1.80 billion.

Analysts said slow retail sales had dealt a blow to Amoy's rental income. "They cut rents for some tenants. They are not making money in a sluggish retail environment," said Raymond Ngai, property analyst at UBS Securities.
He said rental income only grew by 3.1 percent for the year, significantly lower than expectations of five percent growth.
"Retailers are their main source of recurrent rental income and that link has clearly been difficult," added Euan Weir, analyst at Merrill Lynch.
"I think it has been a difficult year because of the retail exposure but I would expect that to improve going into 1997."
Franklin Lam, director of research at HG Asia, said the decline in earnings per share would disappoint some investors.

"Considering the company could be booking artificial profits to beef up the bottom line but did not is in a way a good thing in the sense that they did not want to sell things on the cheap. But it is a bad thing for people who put a premium on continuous earnings growth," he said.

"Most companies put a lot of emphasis on the EPS growth. I think it is either a sign of distress or they do not want to, just for the sake of manufacturing an earnings number, sell things on the market on the cheap," said Lam.
He had expected net profit of HK$1.68 billion for 1995/96 but said he would not be revising down his 1996/97 estimate of HK$1.78 billion.
"The surprises in earnings will be from exceptional disposals and this process should last for the next three years so I don't think there is a need to change the bottom line number," he said.
"Amoy has a proactive management, one that I can count on to sell old assets and buy new assets to rejuvenate the portfolio," Lam added.
